nodes.label: Database Design
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL 15+ on Supabase; 14 tables, 42 RLS policies, 47 indexes. Four principles: normalized not one wide table, the database enforces its own invariants, the ML audit trail is immutable, and features and labels are physically separate.

nodes.label: Normalized Schema, Not One Wide Table
nodes.rationale: A wide table would force NULL-padding for every project missing a dimension, make constraints unenforceable, and turn every write into a lock on one hot row.

nodes.label: profiles Table
nodes.rationale: 1:1 with auth.users, carries role (ADMIN/OFFICER/ANALYST/VIEWER, default VIEWER) plus department and state. Role is never accepted from a client; profiles_update_own_no_role_change blocks self-promotion by comparing the new row against the stored role.

nodes.label: projects Table
nodes.rationale: Central entity with unique project_code, status CHECK, coordinate ranges and ordered date pairs. created_by uses ON DELETE SET NULL so removing a user never destroys project history, and actual_completion_date exists for record-keeping but is deliberately never copied into feature snapshots.

nodes.label: land_acquisition Table
nodes.rationale: 1:1 via UNIQUE project_id. land_award_after_notification and land_possession_after_award encode the statutory sequence notification to award to possession.

nodes.label: compensation Table
nodes.rationale: 1:1 with project; paid <= required enforced; last_updated maintained by its own trigger.

nodes.label: risk_factor_types Lookup Table
nodes.rationale: factor_type is a FK to a lookup table rather than a CHECK because the brief requires new factor types without destructive schema changes - adding one is a single INSERT rather than a constraint rebuild that revalidates the whole table. Closed lifecycle vocabularies (status, severity, role) stay CHECK constraints since they are not expected to grow.

nodes.label: Generated Columns (GENERATED ALWAYS STORED)
nodes.rationale: land_acquisition_percentage, compensation_pending and compensation_pending_percentage. PostgreSQL recomputes on every write and rejects any INSERT/UPDATE targeting the column, so no client, future service, direct SQL session or dashboard admin can spoof a derived value - computing in Node would protect only the path that happens to go through Node. Division is guarded by CASE because a required total of 0 is legitimate. A generated column cannot declare NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, which is stricter than the brief, not weaker.

nodes.label: predictions Table
nodes.rationale: Records an inference attempt. Composite FK (feature_snapshot_id, project_id) makes cross-project attachment structurally impossible, and ON DELETE RESTRICT prevents deleting a snapshot a prediction depends on so the audit trail cannot be silently broken.

nodes.label: predictions_result_matches_status Constraint
nodes.rationale: SUCCESS requires both predicted_delay_days and risk_level; FAILED and PENDING require both NULL. Written as a CASE over the status rather than a chain of ORs, because a CASE with no ELSE returns NULL and a NULL CHECK passes - so a newly added fourth status would slip past unvalidated. Forcing a future author to touch this constraint is the point. risk_level is included because writing 'LOW' would be the same fabrication one column over.

nodes.label: Why 0 Is The Worst Available Placeholder
nodes.rationale: 0 is a valid, plausible 'no delay expected' reading, so a failure stored as 0 renders green on dashboards, drags AVG(predicted_delay_days) down so the more failures the healthier the portfolio looks, and is learned as fact by any training query that forgets to filter on status. A sentinel like -1 violates the >= 0 CHECK and must be remembered by every consumer forever. NULL is the only representation that means 'no value' to the database, to SQL aggregates and to every client library.

nodes.label: Migration 0002 Deliberately Does Not Rewrite Rows
nodes.rationale: It cannot distinguish a fabricated 0 from a genuine 0-day forecast filed under the wrong status, so it aborts and documents the query for finding and clearing them by hand.

nodes.label: Money Precision (NUMERIC 18,2)
nodes.rationale: Exact decimal, never floating point: FLOAT cannot represent 0.10 exactly and accumulates error across sums, which is unacceptable for compensation figures. Rupees to paise; percentages NUMERIC(7,4); areas NUMERIC(14,4); day counts NUMERIC(10,2) because model output is continuous.

nodes.label: NUMERIC Arrives In JavaScript As A Number
nodes.rationale: Corrected after live verification: PostgREST serialises NUMERIC as a JSON number, not a string. Values are correct but a JS double holds integers exactly only to 2^53 while NUMERIC(18,2) permits ~1e16, so the top of the range is not representable. Nothing is currently wrong because no code sums money in JS - derived values are generated columns copied through untouched - but aggregation must stay in SQL or go through a decimal library. Writes accept decimal strings, so the round trip is strings in, numbers out.

nodes.label: The Feature Snapshot Concept
nodes.rationale: A project mutates continuously, so if predictions referenced live rows, reopening a prediction six months later would show today's values rather than the ones the model saw. For a system advising government officials, 'we cannot reconstruct why the model said 287 days' is not an acceptable answer, so project_feature_snapshots freezes the exact feature vector at prediction time.

nodes.label: Snapshot Immutability Enforcement
nodes.rationale: No updated_at column and no UPDATE trigger; no UPDATE policy for any role but ADMIN; ON DELETE RESTRICT on referencing FKs. Consequence: re-running a stored prediction against its stored snapshot reproduces the same input vector however far the live project has moved on.

nodes.label: Data Leakage Prevention
nodes.rationale: Target leakage is the most common way an ML project produces excellent offline metrics and useless real-world predictions, so the schema defends in four independent ways: physical separation, a documented column boundary, elapsed-time features treated as inputs, and a temporal guard trigger.

nodes.label: Physical Feature/Label Separation
nodes.rationale: Features live in project_feature_snapshots and the label in actual_outcomes, so a training query must perform an explicit, reviewable JOIN and a careless SELECT * over the feature table cannot pull the label in by accident.

nodes.label: Documented Snapshot Column Boundary
nodes.rationale: schema.sql carries a header listing what must never be added (delay_days_target, actual delay, actual completion date, realised cost overrun); verified automatically by a naming-pattern audit, with actual_delay_days existing in actual_outcomes and nowhere else.

nodes.label: Elapsed-Time Features Are Inputs, Not Targets
nodes.rationale: notification_delay_days and award_delay_days measure delay already observed as of snapshot_date between past events, so they are legitimate inputs - but must never be computed against a future or projected date.

nodes.label: trg_actual_outcomes_temporal_guard
nodes.rationale: Rejects any outcome whose outcome_date precedes the snapshot_date it labels. A CHECK constraint cannot express this because it spans two tables, so labelling an old snapshot with an earlier observation becomes a database error rather than a silent modelling bug.

nodes.label: Composite Foreign Keys Against Cross-Project Contamination
nodes.rationale: (feature_snapshot_id, project_id) on both predictions and actual_outcomes makes linking a snapshot outside its own project unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged.

nodes.label: actual_outcomes Table
nodes.rationale: The ML target in its own table, UNIQUE on feature_snapshot_id so there is one label per snapshot, carrying the composite FK and the temporal guard.

nodes.label: prediction_explanations Table
nodes.rationale: Per-feature attribution with signed contribution scores, unique per (prediction_id, rank) and (prediction_id, feature_name).

nodes.label: Attribution Is Not Causal Proof
nodes.rationale: Contribution values describe how the model weighted a feature in producing its own output; a high score for title_issue_flag means the model leaned on it, not that the title issue provably caused the delay. UI copy and reports must not present them as proven cause.

nodes.label: model_versions Registry
nodes.rationale: A partial unique index allows at most one ACTIVE model so the serving model is unambiguous. mae, rmse and r2_score are NULLable on purpose - NULL means 'not yet measured' and a plausible-looking substitute is never written. r2_score is capped at 1 with no lower bound because R-squared is genuinely unbounded below.

nodes.label: Index Strategy
nodes.rationale: Explicit indexes added only where a real access path needs them; every index costs write throughput, so columns already covered by a UNIQUE constraint or by the leading column of a composite got none. Composite (project_id, snapshot_date DESC) and (project_id, created_at DESC) serve both plain lookup and the ordered 'latest' query.

nodes.label: Row Level Security Model
nodes.rationale: Enabled on all 14 tables with 42 default-deny policies. OFFICER is scoped to assignments because a field officer's authority is project-specific; ANALYST and VIEWER are read-only oversight roles; snapshots, predictions and outcomes have no OFFICER update policy because they are the audit trail; model_versions is readable by all and writable only by ADMIN because the registry decides which model serves traffic.

nodes.label: SECURITY DEFINER RLS Helper Functions
nodes.rationale: current_app_role(), is_admin() and is_assigned_to_project() read public.profiles, which is itself under RLS - without DEFINER the policy on profiles re-enters itself and recurses until PostgreSQL aborts, the single most common way a Supabase RLS setup breaks. search_path is pinned to public, pg_temp so they cannot be hijacked, and they are defined after the tables they read because a SQL function body is validated at CREATE time.

nodes.label: VIEWER/ANALYST National Scope Decision
nodes.rationale: The brief says 'read-only access according to allowed project visibility' without defining the bound - state, department or an explicit grant list each produce a different schema, and picking one now would hard-code a guess into the most expensive place to guess wrong. Replacement is contained: every affected policy is a SELECT policy containing the literal 'ANALYST','VIEWER', and profiles.state/department already exist to carry the boundary. The RLS tests assert the current scope so narrowing it fails loudly.

nodes.label: RLS Is Not Sufficient On Its Own
nodes.rationale: The Node backend connects with the service role key, which bypasses RLS entirely, so every policy is invisible to backend queries. The backend must resolve role server-side, check assignment before OFFICER writes, reject non-ADMIN role changes, and reserve the service-role client for operations that genuinely need to bypass RLS.

nodes.label: Pre-Production Checklist
nodes.rationale: Define the VIEWER/ANALYST visibility boundary, confirm the OFFICER-narrower-than-VIEWER asymmetry is intended, add the signup profile trigger, audit every service-role route, and re-test the policy matrix against real Supabase Auth JWTs.

nodes.label: Assumptions And Deviations From The Brief
nodes.rationale: Recorded rather than silently invented: OFFICER sees fewer projects than VIEWER (implemented literally, flagged as unusual); national VIEWER/ANALYST read; generated columns cannot carry NOT NULL DEFAULT 0; predicted_delay_days is nullable under a CHECK; factor_type uses a lookup table; extra statuses added; migrations hold no copy of the baseline; demo predictions point at a placeholder model named demo-0.1.0-untrained with NULL metrics; profiles cannot be seeded in SQL because auth.users is Supabase-managed.
